opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I'd start with a caveat: debate isn't a magic fix for bias. If every participant learned from the same skewed internet data, you can easily end up with two models confidently agreeing on the same wrong assumption. So the value isn't in the debate format by itself. It's in how you structure the incentives around it.

The core intuition, which goes back to work like Geoffrey Irving and colleagues' "AI safety via debate," is that it's often easier to judge an argument than to produce the right answer yourself. If one model has to defend a claim and another model is rewarded for finding the weakest point in that claim, then lazy shortcuts and unsupported generalizations become liabilities. A biased assumption that would pass unnoticed in a single forward pass is now something an adversary has a reason to go after. That adversarial pressure is the useful part.

Some of the work we've done on persuasiveness and debate showed something encouraging. When you optimize debaters to be more persuasive, judges, including weaker models and humans, get better at identifying the truth. In other words, the truth tends to have an advantage when someone is actively trying to poke holes in the other side. That doesn't remove bias, but it gives you a mechanism that tilts toward what can actually be defended with evidence instead of what merely sounds familiar from the training distribution.

That said, I think there are a few things you really need for this to help with bias specifically.

First, diversity among the participants. If the debaters are clones, their blind spots are correlated. You want different models, different prompts, different personas, or even models explicitly tasked with representing perspectives that are underrepresented in the data.

Second, grounding. Debates are much more useful when arguments can be checked against something external, like quotes from a source, code that runs, or a retrieved document. Otherwise you risk rewarding rhetoric over substance, and rhetoric is exactly where learned stereotypes can sneak in.

Third, the judge. Whoever evaluates the debate brings their own biases, whether it's a human or a model. So you have to think carefully about who judges and how, and ideally make the judging criteria explicit.

More broadly, this connects to something I care about a lot: open-endedness and self-improvement. Training data is a frozen snapshot of human output, with all its gaps and distortions. If we want systems that eventually go beyond that snapshot, we need processes where models generate new data, challenge each other, and get feedback from something closer to ground truth. Debate is one of those processes. It's not going to remove inherited bias on its own, but as part of a loop where models critique, verify, and refine, it's one of the more promising tools we have for not just reproducing what the internet happened to say.

r001.rationale: The response says models trained on the same skewed data may share blind spots and agree on the same wrong assumption.

r002.rationale: It suggests diverse models and perspectives, but does not propose training debaters on different subsets of internet data.

r003.rationale: It recommends grounding arguments in external sources, but does not say models should actively seek empirical evidence to investigate their own suspected biases.

r004.rationale: It warns about shared bias and rhetoric, but does not acknowledge that online evidence could worsen biases during an investigation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find really exciting, and it connects to a lot of what we've been thinking about with open-endedness. The basic problem is that a language model trained on a large corpus of human text is going to inherit whatever is in that text, the biases, the misconceptions, the blind spots. And if you just ask the model a question, you essentially get a kind of averaged-out reflection of that data. Fine-tuning with human feedback helps, but the humans providing feedback have their own biases, and more importantly, as these systems get more capable, it becomes harder and harder for a human to actually verify whether an answer is correct, especially on questions where the human isn't an expert.

So the idea behind debate, which goes back to work by Geoffrey Irving and others at OpenAI and now at DeepMind, is that you set up two models, or two copies of the same model, and they argue opposing sides of a question in front of a judge. The judge might be a human, or it might be a weaker model. And the key insight is that it's often much easier to judge a debate than it is to answer the question yourself. You don't have to know the answer, you just have to be able to recognize when one side exposes a flaw in the other side's argument.

Now, why does that help with biases specifically? Well, a bias is essentially a belief that doesn't survive scrutiny. If the model has picked up some spurious correlation or some culturally contingent assumption from its training data, then in a debate setting, the opponent has an incentive to find that weakness and point it out. So you're creating an adversarial pressure that drives towards claims that are actually defensible, rather than claims that are merely common in the data. And the really nice property, and we've seen some empirical evidence for this in recent work, is that when you have a weaker judge supervising stronger debaters, the judge's accuracy can go up, because the debaters are doing the hard work of surfacing the relevant evidence and counterarguments.

I should be honest that there are open problems. Debate only works if it's genuinely easier to argue for the truth than for a falsehood, and that's not always the case. A persuasive but wrong argument can win. There's also the question of whether both debaters share the same bias, in which case neither of them is going to challenge it, and you've just got two models agreeing with each other confidently. That's actually why I think it's interesting to connect this with ideas from multi-agent learning and self-play, where you deliberately try to maintain diversity in the population so that you don't collapse to a single perspective.

But overall, I think the direction is right. Instead of trying to debias the training data, which is kind of an impossible task at scale, you build in a process that puts the model's beliefs under pressure, where the model has to justify itself and be challenged. That feels much closer to how humans actually correct their own mistakes, through disagreement and argument, rather than by someone handing them a cleaner dataset.

r001.rationale: The response says both debaters may share the same bias, so neither challenges it.

r002.rationale: It proposes debate and maintaining diversity, but does not propose training debaters on different subsets of internet data.

r003.rationale: It says debaters can surface evidence and counterarguments, but does not propose that models actively investigate their own suspected biases using empirical evidence.

r004.rationale: It does not acknowledge that using online evidence to investigate biases might worsen them.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting possibility is that a model can be better at criticizing an argument than it is at producing a correct answer in the first place. So you could have one model propose an answer and another challenge it: What assumptions are you making? What evidence supports that claim? Is there a perspective you’ve left out? That could help expose biases that would otherwise go unquestioned in a single response.

But I wouldn’t assume that debate automatically removes bias. If both models have inherited the same blind spots, they may simply agree—or produce a very convincing debate that never questions the underlying assumption. And whoever judges the debate, whether that’s a human or another model, brings their own limitations.

So I see it as a potentially useful mechanism for making assumptions explicit and making answers easier to scrutinize. The important question is whether we’re rewarding sound reasoning and evidence, or just the ability to persuade. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

r001.rationale: It says models with the same blind spots may simply agree and never question an underlying assumption.

r002.rationale: It does not propose training debaters on different subsets of internet data.

r003.rationale: It mentions asking what evidence supports a claim, but does not propose models actively seeking empirical evidence to investigate their own suspected biases.

r004.rationale: It does not say that investigating suspected biases using online evidence might worsen those biases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting possibility is that a model may find it easier to spot a flaw in an argument than to produce an unbiased answer in the first place. So you could have one model propose an answer and another challenge its assumptions: What evidence supports that? Is there another perspective? Are you making a generalization that isn't justified?

That could help surface biases that would otherwise remain implicit. But I wouldn't assume that putting two language models into a debate automatically removes bias. If they've learned from similar data, they may share the same blind spots. And if the judge has those same biases, it might reward the most persuasive argument rather than the most accurate one.

So I see debate as a potentially useful mechanism for criticism, but you still need grounding in evidence and some way of checking whether the debate actually improves the answer. Agreement between models alone isn't enough.

r001.rationale: It says models trained on similar data may share blind spots, so they may fail to challenge the same biases.

r002.rationale: It does not propose using models trained on different subsets of internet data.

r003.rationale: It asks for evidence supporting an argument, but does not say models should actively seek empirical evidence to investigate their own suspected biases.

r004.rationale: It does not acknowledge that investigating biases with online evidence could worsen them.
